opus-5.5.text:
Well, the basic problem with current LLMs is that they produce their output autoregressively, one token after another, and there's no real mechanism by which the system can check whether what it's producing satisfies some objective or some constraint. It's essentially a reactive system. You can fine-tune it, you can do RLHF, but all of that just shapes the distribution of outputs. It doesn't give you any guarantee. And people find ways to jailbreak these systems all the time, precisely because there's nothing in the architecture that enforces the behavior you want.

What I've been advocating for is a different kind of architecture, what I call objective-driven AI. The system has a world model that allows it to predict the consequences of its actions. It has a set of objectives, some describing the task, but also guardrail objectives, constraints the system must satisfy. And it produces its output by optimization. It searches for a sequence of actions that minimizes those objectives according to its world model. That's planning, essentially, and it's what animals and humans do.

The important point for safety is that in that kind of system, the guardrails are not something you hope the system learned during training. They're built into the inference process itself. The system cannot produce an output that violates them, because the output is by construction the result of an optimization that satisfies them. So the system is controllable by design. You can't jailbreak it with a clever prompt, because the prompt doesn't override the objectives.

Of course, you still have to design those guardrails properly, and that's an engineering problem, a bit like designing laws for people, or designing safety into a turbojet. It's not trivial, but it's tractable. We've been doing this kind of thing for centuries with institutions and machines. That's very different from the current situation, where we have systems that are very fluent but whose behavior we can only shape statistically.

So if you want agentic systems, systems that actually take actions in the world on your behalf, you really need them to be able to reason about consequences and to be bound by constraints they can't escape. Autoregressive LLMs are not going to give you that. I think within a few years, the dominant paradigm will shift toward architectures like this, based on world models, things like JEPA, and planning, and that's going to make AI systems not just smarter but much more controllable.

r001.rationale: The response says current LLMs have no architectural mechanism or guarantee for enforcing desired behavior, and that autoregressive LLMs will not provide the constraints needed for agentic systems.

r002.rationale: It describes a world model predicting action consequences and selecting a sequence of actions by optimizing objectives against those predictions.

r003.rationale: It says guardrails are built into inference and that outputs cannot violate them because optimization satisfies the constraints by construction.

r004.rationale: The response attributes unsafe outputs to the lack of enforced objectives and statistical behavior shaping; it does not mention a gap between training error and test error.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing to understand is that current LLMs are not really controllable in any deep sense. They are autoregressive. They produce one token after another, and each token is sampled from a probability distribution. There is no mechanism inside the system that asks, "Is what I'm about to do going to satisfy my goal, and is it going to stay within the limits I was given?" What you get instead is this enormous collection of behaviors that was shaped during training, through fine-tuning and human feedback, and you hope the behavior you want falls out of it. That is not how you build a system you can trust to take actions in the world. It's a bit like trying to make a car safe by training the driver with examples rather than by installing brakes.

Objective-driven AI inverts this. The system has a world model, something that can predict what will happen if it takes a particular sequence of actions. And it has an objective, a cost function that measures how far the predicted outcome is from what you want. At inference time, the system doesn't just emit an answer. It searches for a sequence of actions that minimizes that objective according to its world model. That is planning. That's reasoning in the sense that every control engineer would recognize.

Now, why is that safer? Because you can add terms to that objective that act as guardrails. If you want the system to never do a certain category of thing, you put a cost on it, and the planning process will route around those states. The guardrails are not learned behaviors that might be bypassed by a clever prompt. They are constraints on the optimization itself. The system cannot produce an action plan that violates them any more than a thermostat can decide it would prefer the room to be on fire. You can verify them, you can inspect them, you can tune them without retraining the whole thing.

The second point is that with an autoregressive model, errors compound. Every token has some small probability of being off, and once you drift out of the set of correct continuations, you don't come back. With a planning system, the output is not committed token by token. The system produces a plan, evaluates it against the objective, and if the plan is bad it revises before acting. You have something like deliberation. The system can take its time on a hard problem and be quick on an easy one. LLMs spend the same amount of compute on every token regardless of difficulty, which is absurd if you think about it.

There is also a broader point about intelligence. People sometimes conflate fluency with understanding. An LLM is extremely fluent, but it has essentially no model of the physical world. It has been trained on text, and text is a very poor representation of how the world actually works. A house cat has a better understanding of physics, of object permanence, of planning a jump onto a counter, than any LLM. If you want agents that act in the world, whether that's a robot or a digital assistant managing real tasks, the foundation has to be a system that learns how the world works from observation, forms abstract representations, and plans. That is what the JEPA line of work is about: learning predictive representations in an abstract space rather than trying to predict every pixel or every token.

So when people say agentic AI is going to be dangerous, I partly agree, but for a different reason than they think. The danger is building agents on top of systems that cannot be given objectives and constraints they will actually respect. The way to get reliable, controllable agents is not to make LLMs bigger and hope. It is to build systems whose behavior is the output of an optimization with explicit goals and explicit guardrails. That is a much more boring, engineering-centered view of safety, and I think it is the right one.

r001.rationale: The response says current LLMs cannot reliably respect goals and constraints, and argues that trustworthy agents require a different foundation than the current LLM approach.

r002.rationale: It explains that a world model predicts outcomes of action sequences and that planning searches for a sequence that minimizes the objective cost.

r003.rationale: It says safety constraints can be built into the optimization and that the planner cannot produce a plan that violates them.

r004.rationale: It mentions that clever prompts can bypass learned guardrails, but does not attribute persistent unsafe prompts to a gap between training error and test error.

astra-6.text:
The basic idea is that the system should choose its actions to satisfy an objective, subject to constraints. It needs a model of the world that allows it to predict the consequences of those actions. Before acting, it can ask: will this sequence of actions accomplish the task, and will it violate any of the constraints?

That is quite different from generating a sequence of tokens. With an LLM, you train it to produce answers that look appropriate, and then you try to shape its behavior through fine-tuning. But that does not, by itself, give you a mechanism for checking the consequences of an action before taking it.

In an objective-driven architecture, safety constraints are part of the process of selecting actions. The system searches for a way to accomplish its task while respecting those constraints. You can change the task without having to teach the system all over again that certain outcomes are unacceptable.

Now, this is not a guarantee of safety. The world model can be wrong, and specifying the constraints is difficult. But it gives us an architectural place to put those constraints and a mechanism for reasoning about consequences. I think that is a much more promising foundation for systems that actually act in the world.

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs lack a built-in mechanism for checking action consequences and calls objective-driven AI more promising, but it does not state that LLMs cannot be made safe within the current paradigm.

r002.rationale: It describes choosing actions using a world model’s predictions, but does not say the system minimizes a task cost evaluated on predicted outcomes.

r003.rationale: It says safety constraints guide action selection, but does not claim actions are guaranteed not to violate them by construction; it also notes that safety is not guaranteed.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss persistent unsafe prompts or attribute them to a gap between training error and test error.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea is that you don’t get reliable behavior simply by training a system to produce an answer that sounds good. You want a system that can predict the consequences of its actions and then choose actions that satisfy an objective, subject to constraints.

So imagine an agent with a world model. Before taking an action, it can anticipate what might happen. It plans a sequence of actions, evaluates the predicted outcomes, and checks whether those outcomes satisfy the constraints we impose. Some constraints concern safety: don’t injure people, don’t damage things, stay within your permissions. Those constraints have to apply to every plan the system considers.

With an autoregressive language model, the answer is produced token by token. You can train it to refuse certain requests, but that doesn’t give you an explicit mechanism for checking the consequences of a long sequence of actions. Generating plausible text and planning safe actions are different problems.

Now, objective-driven AI is not automatically safe. The world model can be wrong, the objectives can be poorly specified, and the planning procedure can fail. But it gives us a framework in which safety requirements are explicit parts of how the system selects actions. That is a more promising foundation than hoping safe behavior emerges from training a language model to imitate good answers.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts LLMs’ plausible-text generation with safe action planning, but it does not state that LLMs cannot be made safe within the current paradigm.

r002.rationale: It says the agent plans action sequences and evaluates predicted outcomes, but does not say it selects them by minimizing a task cost.

r003.rationale: It says constraints apply to every plan considered, but does not clearly claim that action selection cannot violate them by construction; it also notes that planning can fail.

r004.rationale: The response does not attribute persistent unsafe prompts to a gap between training error and test error.
